questions.q: What makes a vectorized backtest fast compared to an event-driven one?
options: It skips computing returns for most bars
It operates on entire arrays/Series at once using optimized compiled code, instead of looping in Python bar by bar
It only works on weekly data instead of daily data
It avoids using pandas entirely
questions.explain: Vectorized backtests express the whole computation as NumPy/pandas array operations, which run in compiled code — dramatically faster than an interpreted Python loop over each bar.

questions.q: In a vectorized backtest, how is look-ahead bias avoided?
options: It's structurally impossible in vectorized code
By manually shifting the signal forward (e.g. `.shift(1)`) before multiplying by returns
By using a larger rolling window
Vectorized backtests cannot avoid look-ahead bias
questions.explain: Unlike event-driven loops, vectorized code doesn't enforce chronological order automatically — the author must explicitly shift signals forward to prevent a bar's signal from being paired with its own return.

questions.q: Why does an event-driven backtest structurally prevent look-ahead bias?
options: Because it runs faster than a vectorized backtest
Because the strategy object only ever receives data up to the current bar in the loop — future bars haven't been handed to it yet
Because it doesn't use any historical data
Because it always trades at the closing price
questions.explain: The event-driven loop processes bars strictly in order and only exposes data up to the current step, so the strategy has no mechanism to see future data even by accident.

questions.q: Which kind of strategy logic is described as 'path-dependent' and awkward to express in a vectorized backtest?
options: A simple moving-average crossover
A stop-loss that exits based on drawdown since entry, which depends on the sequence of prior prices and the trade's own history
A buy-and-hold strategy
Computing a 20-day rolling average
questions.explain: Path-dependent logic depends on the sequence of what already happened (like a running drawdown since entry), which is hard to express as simple array math but natural in a bar-by-bar loop.

questions.q: What is the typical real-world workflow quant researchers use with these two approaches?
options: Use only event-driven backtests from the start, since they are always better
Use only vectorized backtests, since event-driven backtests are never needed
Vectorize first to quickly explore many ideas, then validate the best candidates with an event-driven backtest for realistic execution
Alternate randomly between the two for every test
questions.explain: Vectorized backtests are used for fast early-stage exploration across many ideas or parameters; event-driven backtests are then used to validate the survivors with more realistic, path-dependent execution modeling.
